hints: Think about where translation happens in the cell and which type of RNA brings the code there to be read.
Recall what each small three-base unit on that RNA is called, and what matching structure on tRNA recognises it.
Remember how the first code triplet is special and how tRNA molecules deliver their amino acids side by side.
Consider what happens after the amino acids are linked and how the ribosome moves on to build a chain 99 amino acids long.
walkthrough:
Set the scene at the ribosome**
Translation does not happen free in the cytoplasm. The mRNA code arrives and attaches to a ribosome. This exposes two codons at a time in the binding sites, ready to be read.

Match codons with anticodons**
Each tRNA carries one specific amino acid. The first tRNA is tRNAmet carrying methionine. Its anticodon binds by complementary base pairing to the codon on mRNA, starting with the START codon AUG.

Hold amino acids together to link them**
A second tRNA with its amino acid binds next to the first. The ribosome holds the two amino acids close together so the enzyme peptidyl transferase can form a peptide bond between them.

Elongate and finish the chain**
After bond formation the first tRNA detaches and can be reused. The ribosome moves along one codon, elongation repeats, until a STOP codon is reached and the 99-amino-acid polypeptide is released.

Final answer: mRNA attaches to a ribosome exposing two codons; tRNA molecules each carrying a specific amino acid bind via anticodon to complementary codon, starting at START codon AUG; two amino acids are held close together so a peptide bond forms; ribosome moves along one codon and process repeats until STOP codon when polypeptide is released.

hints: Start by listing where the two types of bond form - along the backbone to make the chain, or folding the chain by linking side chains.
Think about which chemical groups are joined in a peptide bond compared with which parts of the amino acids interact in tertiary folding.
Compare bond strength - which type is a strong covalent link and which tertiary bonds are weaker and more easily broken by heat.
walkthrough:
Find one similarity**
Both levels of structure use strong links. Like a peptide bond, a disulfide bond in tertiary structure is also covalent. That is the main similarity to state.

Contrast the location of the bonds**
A peptide bond always links the backbone: carboxyl group of one amino acid to amino group of the next, forming the primary chain. Tertiary bonds are different - they form between R groups of amino acids that may be far apart in the sequence, folding the chain into 3D shape.

Contrast the type and strength**
Apart from disulfide, tertiary bonds are hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions. These are weaker than the covalent peptide bond and less resistant to heat. So peptide bonds give the backbone its strength while tertiary bonds give flexible 3D stability.

Final answer: Similarity: peptide bond and disulfide bond are both covalent bonds; Difference: peptide bond is between COOH of one amino acid and NH2 of adjacent amino acid, whereas tertiary bonds are between R groups / side chains; tertiary bonds include hydrogen, ionic and hydrophobic interactions which are not covalent and are weaker / less thermostable than peptide bonds.

hints: Look at Fig. 3.1 - notice the active site is enclosed by flaps and the question tells you those flaps are flexible.
Recall the difference between lock and key and induced fit - does the active site stay rigid or change shape when substrate arrives.
Think about what the movement of the flaps achieves for fit and for forming the enzyme-substrate complex.
walkthrough:
Use the flexible flaps**
In Fig. 3.1 the active site sits in the middle enclosed by the flap region. Because the flaps are flexible they can open to let the large polyprotein substrate enter, then close round it.

Apply induced fit, not lock and key**
The substrate is not fully complementary to the active site at first. On binding, the active site changes shape and moulds around the substrate. This is the key idea of induced fit.

Get a perfect fit for catalysis**
The shape change gives a fully complementary fit and forms the enzyme-substrate complex. This close fit strains bonds and lowers activation energy so HIV protease can cut the polyprotein.

Final answer: Flap region opens to allow polyprotein substrate to enter then closes around it; active site changes shape / moulds around substrate; substrate becomes fully complementary / better fit allowing enzyme-substrate complex formation.

hints: The drug is described as similar to the normal polyprotein substrate - what does that suggest about where it will try to bind.
If the drug occupies that site instead of the real substrate, what happens to cutting of the polyprotein and production of new viruses.
walkthrough:
Recognise competitive inhibition**
Because indinavir has a similar shape to the polyprotein substrate, it competes for and binds to the active site of HIV protease instead of the substrate. It blocks entry of the real substrate so no enzyme-substrate complex can form.

Link to therapeutic effect**
With the active site blocked, HIV protease cannot cut the polyprotein into separate functioning proteins needed for replication. Fewer new viral proteins means viral replication is stopped, which is why it works as an anti-retroviral drug.

Final answer: Indinavir acts as a competitive inhibitor binding to the active site instead of polyprotein substrate, preventing enzyme-substrate complex formation; polyprotein is not cut into functional proteins so viral replication is prevented.
